Overview and Management of Bone
Tumors

FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify appropriate surgical management of benign and malignant bone tumors.
Describe the surgical principles of benign bone tumor excision.
Describe the surgical principles of malignant bone tumor excision.
Identify surgical adjuvants used to treat benign and malignant bone tumors.
Overview
Tumor histology and biologic activity
The surgical management of benign and malignant bone tumors depends on the histologic
diagnosis and the associated biologic activity of each lesion.




NOTES
SEND FEEDBACK

1/18

As tumor biologic activity increases, the histologic grade of a tumor appears to be higher,
with increased mitotic activity, necrosis, and cellular atypia and pleomorphism.
Benign aggressive and malignant tumors are associated with a higher risk of local recurrence
and/or metastatic spread, which necessitates wider excision and the use of surgical
adjuvants to reduce these risks.
Extent of surgical excision
The type of surgical excision must balance the risks of the tumor biology or recurrence and
the morbidity associated with the procedure.
Morbidity increases with the spectrum of excision types: Radical excision > wide excision >
marginal excision >intralesional excision
Adjuvant treatment options may reduce the rate of local recurrence postoperatively and
influence the morbidity associated with the procedure.
For malignant tumors, chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy may be used as neoadjuvant
or adjuvant therapy.
For benign tumors, liquid nitrogen, argon beam coagulation, phenol, and hydrogen peroxide
may be used.
Surgical Procedure
Indications
Benign aggressive bone tumors may require surgical excision because of associated bony
destruction, impending pathologic fracture, and/or pain.
Wide surgical excision is required for primary malignant bone tumors to achieve a cure.
Contraindications
Asymptomatic latent benign bone tumors often can be monitored and managed nonsurgically.
Metastatic malignant bone tumors do not always require surgical excision if the procedure will
not be curative and if the tumors do not pose a risk for pathologic fracture.
Palliative adjuvant therapy may be considered to stabilize metastatic disease if surgical
management is not mandated.
Resection Types
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
2/18

Surgical margins are designed to reduce the risk of local recurrence and unnecessary
morbidity.
Adjuvant Therapy
Chemotherapy (Resource 1)
May be administered preoperatively or postoperatively to kill micrometastatic disease and
improve overall survival
Most common mechanism of action is to induce programmed cell death (apoptosis)
Most commonly administered for Ewing sarcoma, osteosarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma;
however, it also may be used to manage other bone and soft-tissue sarcomas and in patients
with metastatic disease.
Chemotherapeutic agents achieve apoptosis via various methods.
Directly damaging DNA: alkylating agents, platinum compounds, anthracyclines
Depleting cellular building blocks: antifolates, cytidine analogs, 5-fluoropyrimidines
Interfering with microtubule function: vinca alkaloids, taxanes
Denosumab
Monoclonal antibody that binds to receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand
Has been used in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting for the management of giant cell
tumor
Radiation therapy
May be administered preoperatively, intraoperatively, or postoperatively to decrease the rate
of local recurrence
Radiation causes DNA damage via the production of free radicals or direct genetic damage
(Resource 2).

Adjuvant Therapy
Denosumab has been administered in the neoadjuvant setting to achieve ossification of
giant cell tumor before curettage and as definitive management for giant cell tumors
that are unresectable and/or metastatic. Errani et al1 reported a local recurrence rate of
60% in 25 patients treated via curettage and denosumab and 16% in 222 patients
treated via curettage alone. The joint preservation rates were 80% versus 94%,

3/18

respectively. Therefore, denosumab should be used selectively in the neoadjuvant
setting or for definitive management if surgical resection is deemed too morbid.
Preoperative Planning
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs of the affected limb
Chest radiograph and/or chest CT scan to examine for metastatic disease
MRI: detailed cross-sectional imaging to plan resection of benign and malignant bone tumors
CT: helpful for diagnosis of osteoid osteoma and for surgical planning
Positron emission tomography/CT: assessment of metabolic activity of bone tumors and
identification of sites of metastatic disease
Whole-body bone scan: assessment of activity associated with bone tumors
Patient Positioning
Patient positioning strategy should account for the surgical approach, exposure, the need for
intraoperative imaging, and any planned fixation or reconstruction.
Surgical Approaches
Considerations for surgical approach
The need to limit tumor contamination of the surgical field
The need to protect neurovascular structures
Surgical fixation and/or reconstruction
Standard surgical approaches may be considered for excision of benign and malignant bone
tumors.
If malignant bone tumors are excised, the biopsy tract also should be excised.
Intraoperative Techniques
Benign Processes/Tumors
Observation: used for asymptomatic inactive/latent bone tumors
Aspiration and injection

Unicameral bone cysts
Methylprednisolone acetate
Bone marrow
Synthetic bone grafts
Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Methylprednisolone acetate
Aneurysmal bone cyst
Calcitonin and methylprednisolone acetate
Doxycycline foam
Curettage
The margin is always intralesional.
Benign tumors commonly managed via curettage and a local adjuvant
Giant cell tumor (high-speed burr and argon beam coagulation or liquid nitrogen)2
Chondroblastoma
Chondromyxoid fibroma3
Osteoblastoma
Aneurysmal bone cyst4
Recurrent unicameral bone cyst
Enchondroma/low-grade chondrosarcoma
Symptomatic fibrous dysplasia (plate or nail fixation)
Surgical adjuvants
Used for benign bone tumors prone to local recurrence (eg, giant cell tumor)
Margin always is intralesional
For aggressive benign lesions managed in this manner, extended intralesional curettage
may involve the use of mechanical, thermal, and chemical adjuvants to minimize the risk of
recurrence (eg, giant cell tumor of bone).
Phenol
Strong base that coagulates proteins
Potential soft-tissue injury with spillage
Liquid nitrogen
Freezes up to 1 cm of tissue
High rate of associated stress fracture (at least 25%)
Argon beam coagulation
Hydrogen peroxide

Materials used for reconstruction of the defect
Polymethyl methacrylate (bone cement): often used for giant cell tumors
Bone graft: freeze-dried allograft, synthetic graft5 (eg, coralline hydroxyapatite6), autologous
graft
Excision/resection
Removal of the lesion and surrounding involved bone with the intent to definitively remove
all tumor
Benign, nonaggressive processes managed via excision/resection without reconstruction
Osteochondroma
Periosteal chondroma
Prophylactic fixation or reconstruction
Giant cell tumor
Osteoblastoma

Benign Processes/Tumors
Benign aggressive lesions involving major bone destruction, soft-tissue extension,
cartilage loss, or fracture may require plate fixation to augment the bone after excision
or, if remaining bone is insufficient, may require reconstruction with the use of a
prosthesis and/or allograft (Resource 3).
Malignant Bone Tumors (Bone Sarcomas)
Overview
Primary malignant bone tumors must be removed with a wide margin to prevent local
recurrence.
A high risk of systemic metastases exists with high-grade tumors.
Surgical management (Resource 4)
Hemipelvectomy (Resource 5)
Hindquarter amputation/external hemipelvectomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
6/18

May be indicated if the tumor involves two or more of the following major structures:
external iliac vessels, femoral/sciatic nerves, hip joint
Despite involvement in one major structure, the limb often can be salvaged via vascular
bypass, reconstruction, or external bracing; however, the decision is made on a case-by-
case basis and in combination with the patient’s wishes.
Internal hemipelvectomy (Resource 6)
Types
Type 1: resection of the iliac wing
Type 2: resection of the periacetabulum
Type 3: resection of the inferior and superior pubic rami, ischium
Type 4: includes the sacrum
Reconstruction versus no reconstruction after internal hemipelvectomy
Controversy exists on whether to reconstruct the pelvis after internal hemipelvectomy.7
Some surgeons report improved functional ability after pelvic reconstruction with the
use of allograft or a custom endoprosthesis; however, this approach is associated with a
higher rate of surgical complications, such as infection and blood loss, and a higher risk
of future revision procedures.
Custom implants can be created to reconstruct periacetabular resections. Small case
series have reported better functional results with this approach than with older
reconstruction options, such as saddle prosthesis and cement-rebar constructs.8,9
Limb salvage surgery (Resource 7): removal of the malignant tumor with a satisfactory
margin and preservation of the limb
The use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, improved modular implants, and cross-sectional
imaging has made limb salvage surgery possible in 85% to 95% of patients with extremity
primary bone sarcoma.
In a landmark 1986 study, Simon et al10 demonstrated no difference in overall survival
between three surgical groups treated via limb salvage surgery, above-knee amputation, or
hip disarticulation for distal femur osteosarcoma. These findings have been replicated in
larger retrospective studies.11
Limb salvage surgery involves wide resection of the tumor followed by durable
reconstruction. Several reconstructive methods can be used based on the patient’s age, the
location of the tumor, and the surgeon’s experience.
Metallic endoprosthesis (Resource 8)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
7/18

Most widely used reconstruction technique often coupled with joint arthroplasty;
considered to be durable with predictable outcomes.
Cemented stems, press-fit stem, and compressive osseointegration can be used to
anchor the implant to bone.
Rate of failure increases with time; infection and aseptic loosening are the most
common modes of failure.12
Custom intercalary endoprostheses are available for diaphyseal sarcomas. Similar to all
endoprostheses, custom intercalary endoprostheses are associated with a risk for
infection and loosening; care should be taken to avoid malrotation.
Allograft (Resource 9)
Intercalary versus osteoarticular
Osteoarticular allografts are a good option because they preserve the healthy side of
the joint and offer ligamentous reconstruction. They are associated with a high rate of
failure because of fracture, infection, nonunion, and early arthritis. Many allograft
reconstructions can be salvaged with the use of an endoprosthesis.13,14
Allograft-prosthetic composite
Combination of an allograft and a total joint replacement
Advantage of using an allograft to restore the bone and ligaments with the use of an off-
the-shelf arthroplasty implant to provide stability, with the best results reported in the
proximal humerus15 and the proximal femur
Vascularized fibula
Can be used with an allograft to promote union or as a biologic reconstruction option in
children, in whom hypertrophy of the fibula is expected
High rates of early complications and revision surgery but overall high rate of union and
lower rates of infections and long-term complications with good functional outcomes16
Bone transport: a newer technique for biologic reconstruction of diaphyseal defects17
Avoids the long-term complications of endoprosthetic and allograft reconstruction by
promoting host bone growth to fill the defect via distraction osteogenesis
May involve the use of internal lengthening nails and external fixators
Several months and multiple surgical procedures often are required to achieve bony
union, which has dissuaded some surgeons from adopting the technique
Amputation: removal of the tumor with a wide or radical margin and removal of the limb
(Resource 10)

8/18

Indicated if neurovascular structures are involved with the tumor or in patients with a
pathologic fracture who have poor response to and absent callus formation after
neoadjuvant chemotherapy
Newer techniques in amputation surgery, management of phantom pain, and prosthetic
design are improving function for amputees.
Osseointegration18
Direct bone anchorage of an external prosthesis
Improves osseoperception and avoids problems associated with poor socket fit
Most helpful for short residual limbs at the transfemoral level
Ertl below-knee amputation: provides a tibial-fibular synostosis that limits motion of the
residual limb
Targeted muscle reinnervation19
Has shown promise in reducing neuropathic pain after amputation
Can be performed at the time of index amputation or in a staged fashion
Rotationplasty
A potential above-knee amputation that is transitioned to a functional below-knee
amputation
The distal femur, knee, and proximal tibia are resected; the sciatic nerve and the popliteal
vessels are preserved.
The distal tibia, ankle, and foot are then rotated 180° and fixed to the femur.
The ankle joint then functions as a knee joint.
Associated with advantages over standard above-knee amputation
Functioning knee joint
No phantom pain because the nerves to the foot are preserved
Allows for high-impact activity
Viable option resulting in excellent functional outcomes in children with distal femur
sarcoma who have considerable growth remaining
Treatment algorithms
Wide resection alone with no role for chemotherapy or radiation therapy
Chondrosarcoma
Adamantinoma
Parosteal osteosarcoma
Low-grade intramedullary osteosarcoma
Chemotherapy plus surgical management (Resource 1)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
9/18

Used to kill micrometastases in the pulmonary parenchyma and systemic circulation
(neoadjuvant chemotherapy)
Delivered as a chemotherapy sandwich—that is, neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by
local control (surgical management with or without radiation therapy) followed by adjuvant
chemotherapy
An integral component of management for the following malignancies:
Osteosarcoma
Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor
Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (malignant fibrous histiocytoma) of bone
Radiation therapy: external beam irradiation can be used for definitive or supplemental
control in the following primary malignant bone tumors (Resource 2):
Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor
Often used as primary local control for sacral or pelvic Ewing sarcoma if surgical morbidity
is deemed too high
Can be used as an adjuvant treatment option postoperatively with close margins
Primary lymphoma of bone
Hemangioendothelioma
Solitary plasmacytoma of bone
Chordoma
In the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting with close margins
Newer radiation therapy techniques, such as proton beam radiation therapy, show
promise and can provide adequate local control, especially in older patients.20

Malignant Bone Tumors (Bone Sarcomas)
The primary surgical objective is to achieve margin-negative resection. If possible, limb
salvage surgery is the preferred treatment option; however, amputation and
rotationplasty are indicated in specific instances.
Malignant tumors that involve the pelvis and require surgical resection can be managed
via internal hemipelvectomy (limb salvage pelvic resection) with or without
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
10/18

reconstruction. In some patients, an external hemipelvectomy (hindquarter amputation)
is required.
Postoperative Management
After curettage or the creation of a cortical defect, weight bearing is protected for 6 to 12
weeks to allow for sufficient healing and to avoid fracture. If plate fixation or cementation was
used, this time may be shortened.
After wide surgical excision, weight bearing and return to activities depends on the type of
reconstruction performed and on whether bony osseointegration is required.
Radiographs are commonly used to gauge bony healing and to monitor for evidence of
recurrent neoplasm.
MRI, CT, and even positron emission tomography/CT may be performed to assess if concern
for recurrent disease exists but may be affected by metal artifact.
Surveillance schedule is determined based on histologic findings.
Benign tumors with increased risk of local recurrence are followed for at least 2 to 3 years.
Malignant tumors are followed in 3-month intervals for the first 2 years, then every 6 months
for 2 years, and then annually. Patients with an endoprosthesis are followed indefinitely
given the risk of implant failure over time.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Surgical excision should not be performed until adequate preoperative imaging studies and a
confirmed histologic diagnosis are obtained.
Surgical management and/or excision of benign and malignant bone tumors should be
performed only by surgeons who are trained in oncologic surgical techniques and in the
management of complications and associated conditions.
Preparation and backup plans are necessary in case intraoperative complications, such as
fracture or damage to surrounding neurovascular structures, occur.
Complications
Benign Tumors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
11/18

Fracture, infection, cellulitis, pulmonary embolism, neurovascular injury or neuropraxia, and
tumor recurrence are possible complications after tumor curettage and the use of adjuvants
and bone filler.21
Malignant Tumors
Local recurrence is a risk after wide resection for a primary bone sarcoma regardless of the
reconstruction method. Damage to nearby neurovascular structures, blood loss requiring
transfusion, and infection also are risks regardless of the reconstruction technique.
Specific surgical complications and the timing of complications depend on the reconstruction
method.
Large endoprosthetic reconstruction is associated with a risk for infection, estimated to be
approximately 10% for lower extremity reconstruction;22 implant loosening; periprosthetic
fractures; and implant failure (Resources 11, 12, 13 and 14).
Henderson et al12 performed a retrospective review of 2,174 endoprosthetic reconstruction
procedures for bone tumors from five institutional databases, reporting the following
findings:
24.5% rate of failure
Failures classified into five distinct categories
Soft-tissue failure
Aseptic loosening
Structural failure
Infection
Local recurrence
Most common mode of failure was infection followed by aseptic loosening
Allograft reconstructions is associated with a risk for infection, allograft fracture, nonunion,
subsidence, and arthritis (Resource 9).
Outcomes
Benign Bone Tumors
Patient outcomes for benign bone tumors and conditions depend on underlying histology.
Benign aggressive tumors, such as giant cell tumor, aneurysmal bone cyst, and
chondroblastoma, may recur, leading to additional surgical procedure and morbidity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:32 PM
AAOS | Overview and Management of Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000516
12/18

Surveillance imaging for a minimum of 2 to 3 years is recommended to monitor for recurrent
disease.
Malignant Bone Tumors
5-year survival rate after amputation or limb salvage for localized extremity osteosarcoma is
greater than 70%, according to studies utilizing data from the National Cancer Institute’s
Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program.23,24
Margin status is an important predictor of local recurrence and survival,25 with a positive
margin being predictive of a local recurrence and poorer overall survival.

Malignant Bone Tumors
Despite advances in surgical technique and reconstruction options, long-term physical
function after limb salvage and amputation for sarcomas in extremities is less than that
in healthy controls; however, studies show no long-term difference in function between
patients who underwent amputation versus limb salvage.26 In addition, health-related
quality-of-life scores assessing mental function show no difference between survivors of
sarcoma and the general population.27
Mark as Complete
